difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE because it is a routine program trace with a few steps (two loop iterations of set difference/union updates) that hinges on one linked concept, simultaneous tuple assignment, taking about 2 minutes for a prepared student.

solution.quick: Trace with **simultaneous** tuple assignment. Iteration 1: the first `if` gives `A={"this"}, B={"that"}, C={"other"}`, and the second `if` gives `A={"other","this"}, B={"this","that"}, C={"that","other"}`. Iteration 2: the first `if` gives `A={"other"}, B={"this"}, C={"that"}`, and the second `if` is skipped. Now `"other"` is not in `C`, so the loop stops and only `B` contains `"this"`: option **(B)**.

steps.title: The semantics that matter
steps.body:
- `X - Y` is **set difference**: the elements of `X` that are not in `Y`. `X | Y` is **set union**.
- `A,B,C = e1,e2,e3` is **simultaneous (tuple) assignment**: Python evaluates all three right-hand expressions using the **old** values of `A`, `B`, `C`, then assigns them together.
- Inside the loop body the two `if` statements run one after the other in the same iteration, so the second `if` sees the values produced by the first.
- The `while` condition `"other" in C` is checked only at the top of each iteration.

steps.title: Iteration 1
steps.body:
Start: `A={"this","that"}`, `B={"that","other"}`, `C={"other","this"}`. The loop test `"other" in C` is true.

**First `if`:** `"this" in A` is true.

- `A-B = {"this","that"} - {"that","other"} = {"this"}`
- `B-C = {"that","other"} - {"other","this"} = {"that"}`
- `C-A = {"other","this"} - {"this","that"} = {"other"}`

Now `A={"this"}`, `B={"that"}`, `C={"other"}`.

**Second `if`:** `"that" in B` is true.

- `C|A = {"other","this"}`
- `A|B = {"this","that"}`
- `B|C = {"that","other"}`

End of iteration 1: `A={"other","this"}`, `B={"this","that"}`, `C={"that","other"}`.

steps.title: Iteration 2
steps.body:
The loop test `"other" in C` is true (`C={"that","other"}`).

**First `if`:** `"this" in A` is true.

- `A-B = {"other","this"} - {"this","that"} = {"other"}`
- `B-C = {"this","that"} - {"that","other"} = {"this"}`
- `C-A = {"that","other"} - {"other","this"} = {"that"}`

Now `A={"other"}`, `B={"this"}`, `C={"that"}`.

**Second `if`:** `"that" in B` is **false** (`B={"this"}`), so it is skipped.

steps.title: Loop exit and the answer
steps.body:
The loop test is checked again: `"other" in C` with `C={"that"}` is **false**, so the loop ends.

| Point in execution | `A` | `B` | `C` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| start | {this, that} | {that, other} | {other, this} |
| iter 1, after 1st `if` | {this} | {that} | {other} |
| iter 1, after 2nd `if` | {other, this} | {this, that} | {that, other} |
| iter 2, after 1st `if` | {other} | {this} | {that} |
| iter 2, 2nd `if` skipped; loop exits | {other} | {this} | {that} |

At the end, `"this"` is in `B` only. The answer is option **(B)**.

solution.teaching:
**Python sets.** A `set` is an unordered collection of distinct, hashable items, written `{"x", "y"}`. The membership test `item in S` is true when `item` belongs to `S`. The operators mirror set algebra:

- `S | T`: union (in either set),
- `S & T`: intersection (in both),
- `S - T`: difference (in `S` but not in `T`),
- `S ^ T`: symmetric difference (in exactly one).

These operators build **new** sets; they do not modify the operands.

**Tuple (simultaneous) assignment.** In `A,B,C = A-B, B-C, C-A`, the right-hand side is a tuple expression. Python evaluates the whole tuple first, using the current values of `A`, `B` and `C`, and only then unpacks it into the three names. The familiar swap `a, b = b, a` works for exactly this reason. Writing the same update as three separate statements (`A = A-B`, then `B = B-C`, then `C = C-A`) is **not** equivalent, because the later lines would see the already-updated `A`.

**Tracing loops.** For a `while` loop, check the condition, run the whole body (every statement in order, each seeing the effects of the previous ones), then check the condition again. A trace table with one row per update is the safest way to do this under exam pressure.

**Back to this question.** Initially each string lies in exactly two of the three sets. The first `if` keeps, for each set, only the element it does not share with the next set in the cycle (`A` with `B`, `B` with `C`, `C` with `A`), so each set shrinks to one element. The second `if` then merges neighbours again. After two iterations the state is `A={"other"}`, `B={"this"}`, `C={"that"}`. `B` no longer contains `"that"` (so the second `if` is skipped) and `C` no longer contains `"other"` (so the loop exits). Only `B` holds `"this"`.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: At the end `A={"other"}`, so `A` does not contain `"this"`. "Only `A`" describes the state after the **first** assignment of iteration 1 (`A={"this"}`), not the final state.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: The loop ends with `A={"other"}`, `B={"this"}`, `C={"that"}`, so `"this"` is in `B` and in no other set.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: At the end `C={"that"}` (which is exactly why the loop condition `"other" in C` fails), so `C` does not contain `"this"`.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: `A` and `C` both contain `"this"` only in the **initial** state (`A={"this","that"}`, `C={"other","this"}`). The loop body runs twice and changes all three sets, so this is not the final state.

solution.commonTrap: Executing `A,B,C=A-B,B-C,C-A` as three sequential assignments, so that `C-A` uses the new `A`. The trace then differs: after iteration 1 you get `A={"other","this"}`, `B=C={"other","that","this"}`, from iteration 2 on `A` and `B` are empty while `C` keeps `"other"`, and the loop would never terminate. Python evaluates the whole right-hand tuple before assigning. Another slip is forgetting that the second `if` runs in the same iteration as the first, using the freshly updated sets.

answerVerification.notes: Hand trace: the loop runs twice. Iteration 1 applies both updates; in iteration 2 only the first applies. The final state is A={'other'}, B={'this'}, C={'that'}. Running the transcribed code in Python 3 (with a print added per iteration) gives the same final state, and only B contains "this". This agrees with the official key B.
